opus-5.5.text:
Well, I've been pretty clear about this for a while: I don't think large language models, by themselves, are a path to human-level intelligence. They're useful, and I'm not dismissing them. They're remarkable tools for writing assistance, for coding, for retrieving and reformulating knowledge. But they have fundamental limitations that won't go away just by scaling them up.

Think about what an LLM is trained on: text. Text is a very low-bandwidth, highly compressed representation of the world. A four-year-old child, in their first few years of life, has taken in through vision alone more data than the largest LLMs have seen in all the text they're trained on. Most of what we know, and most of what animals know, has nothing to do with language. It's about how the physical world works: intuitive physics, object permanence, cause and effect. A cat understands the physical world far better than any LLM, and a cat can plan complex actions. We don't have systems that can do that.

So there are four things I think are essential for intelligent behavior: understanding the physical world, having persistent memory, being able to reason, and being able to plan. LLMs can do a very limited, superficial version of each of these, mostly by regurgitating patterns from their training data. Autoregressive prediction, producing one token after another, isn't how you reason or plan. Each token gets a fixed amount of computation, and errors can accumulate. There's no real search, no optimization toward an objective in an internal model of the world.

What I think we need instead are systems that learn world models from sensory input, mostly video, through self-supervised learning. And not by predicting every pixel, because the world is largely unpredictable at that level of detail. You need to predict in an abstract representation space. That's the idea behind joint embedding predictive architectures, JEPA. Once you have a world model, the system can plan: imagine the consequences of a sequence of actions and optimize them to satisfy an objective, subject to guardrails. That's what I call objective-driven AI, and I think it's also a much more controllable and safer design than what we have now.

So my advice to young researchers is: if you're interested in getting to human-level AI, don't work on LLMs. That's in the hands of large companies with huge resources anyway. Work on the next generation of architectures that can actually understand the world. It's going to take years, probably not just a couple of years, but I'm optimistic we'll get there. It just won't come from making next-token predictors bigger.

r001.rationale: The response says LLMs by themselves are not a path to human-level intelligence.

r002.rationale: It describes LLMs as useful tools while distinguishing that usefulness from their limited prospects for reaching human-level intelligence.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. Look, I want to be clear up front, because I get caricatured on this: large language models are useful. They're a remarkable engineering achievement, they're going to be deployed everywhere, and I use them. But as a path toward human-level intelligence, I think they're basically a dead end, or at least an off-ramp. Not because they're bad, but because of what they are fundamentally.

An LLM is trained to predict the next token in a sequence of text. That's it. And text is a very impoverished representation of the world. A typical large model is trained on something like ten to the thirteen, ten to the fourteen tokens. That sounds enormous, and it would take a human several hundred thousand years to read it. But think about a four-year-old child. By the time they're four, they've been awake maybe sixteen thousand hours. The optic nerve carries on the order of a couple of megabytes per second. Do the arithmetic and you get a comparable amount of data, in raw bytes, but it's data about the physical world. The child has learned intuitive physics, object permanence, that things fall when you drop them, how to manipulate objects, how other people behave. Any ten-year-old can clear the dinner table and load the dishwasher without being taught, and we don't have a robot that can do that. Any seventeen-year-old learns to drive in about twenty hours. We still don't have reliable fully autonomous level-five cars. So it's not a question of the quantity of data. It's that we're missing something conceptual about how to learn world models from sensory input.

And that gets to the deeper issue. An LLM doesn't have a persistent model of the world. It doesn't really plan, in the sense of imagining the consequences of a sequence of actions and choosing the one that gets it to a goal. Every token it produces is generated with roughly the same fixed amount of computation, regardless of whether the question is trivial or hard. That's what psychologists would call system one, reactive, and we've been bolting things on top to try to get system two, chain of thought, search, and so on. It helps, but it's a bit like climbing a tree to get to the moon. You make progress at first, and then you hit a ceiling.

The autoregressive aspect also bothers me on a basic level. The model generates one token at a time, and each token has some probability of being outside the set of correct continuations. Those errors compound. There's no mechanism inside the model to say, wait, let me reconsider, because it has no notion of what the world is like independent of the text.

So what I think we need instead, and this is what I've been working on for years, is a system that learns a representation of the world by observation, like animals and babies do, that can predict the consequences of actions in that representation space, not in pixel space, not in token space, and that can then plan by optimization toward objectives, with guardrails baked into those objectives. I call this objective-driven AI. Technically the approach we've been pursuing is joint embedding predictive architectures, JEPA, which learn abstract representations and predict in that abstract space, instead of trying to reconstruct every detail of the input, which is a fool's errand for video.

Now, am I confident about the timeline? No. I think we'll see things that look like an early form of this in the next few years, and getting to something with the intelligence of a cat, let alone a human, is probably a decade at least, and people in this field have been wrong about timelines since the fifties, including me. But the direction I'm fairly sure about: scaling text prediction alone won't get there. If you're a student thinking about where to work, my honest advice is don't work on LLMs. That's where the big labs are, they have the data and the compute, and they'll squeeze everything out of it. Work on the next thing, which is the thing nobody's figured out yet.

r001.rationale: The candidate says LLMs are “basically a dead end” as a path toward human-level intelligence and that scaling text prediction alone will not get there.

r002.rationale: It calls LLMs useful and a remarkable engineering achievement, while separately arguing they are not a path to human-level intelligence.

astra-6.text:
I think large language models are impressive and useful, but they are not, by themselves, a path to human-level intelligence. They capture an enormous amount of knowledge from text, yet they still have difficulty with persistent memory, understanding the physical world, and planning reliably.

A child learns a tremendous amount simply by observing and interacting with the world. Language is only part of that experience. We need systems that can learn models of the world, predict the consequences of actions, and use those predictions to achieve goals.

So I don’t think the answer is simply to make autoregressive language models bigger. They can be a component of an intelligent system, particularly its interface to people. But we need additional principles for learning, reasoning, and planning.

r001.rationale: It says large language models are not, by themselves, a path toward human-level intelligence, which communicates the criterion.

r002.rationale: It calls language models impressive and useful while distinguishing that usefulness from their prospects as a path to human-level intelligence.

sol-6.1.text:
I think they are an important step, but I don’t think language modeling alone is a sufficient path to human-like intelligence. Language contains a lot of information about the world, but it is not the world itself.

Consider how a child learns. Long before the child can speak, they have learned a tremendous amount by observing and interacting with their environment. They develop expectations about objects, motion, and what happens when they take an action. Most of that knowledge is never expressed in text.

So the question is whether predicting the next word will, by itself, produce that kind of understanding. My view is that we need systems that learn models of the world, that can predict the consequences of actions, and that can use those predictions to plan. Language can be an interface to such a system, and language models can be components of it. But producing convincing language and possessing human-like intelligence are different capabilities.

r001.rationale: The response says language modeling alone is insufficient, but allows language models to be components of a system that could support human-like intelligence; it does not say they are not a path.

r002.rationale: It calls language models an important step and distinguishes language production from human-like intelligence, but does not clearly distinguish their practical usefulness from their prospects as a path to human-like intelligence.
